name: Michael Dell
title: The Boy Who Out-Earned His Teacher
subtitle: How a Houston teenager who mined marriage records started a computer company in his dorm room with $1,000, stepped away, came back, and rebuilt it for the age of AI.
hook: At ==16==, Michael Dell took a job selling newspaper subscriptions by phone, and he noticed that the people who said yes were usually moving house or getting married. Marriage-licence applications were public in Texas. So he hired his friends, collected the addresses from the ==16 counties== around Houston, and mailed each couple a free trial offer. He made about **$18,000** in one year. When a school assignment asked for a tax return, he handed in his real one, and his teacher told him it had to be wrong: "You made more money than I did!" In November 2026, Forbes put his fortune at ==$228.5 billion==.

chapters.title: The Boy in the Red Bathrobe

blocks.text: A woman from a testing company turned up at a house in the suburbs of Houston, Texas. She said she was there to see "Mr. Michael Dell." His mother told her he was taking a bath, and that she would let him know he had a visitor. Then Mr. Dell appeared. He was ==eight years old==, still damp, and wearing a red terrycloth bathrobe.

Here is how that strange meeting came about. Michael had seen an ad in one of his parents' magazines. It promised a high school diploma if you passed "one simple test." Texas Monthly says he clipped the form from the back of the magazine and applied. He was in third grade, and he wanted to cut about nine years off his schooling so he could get on with business.
When I was in third grade, I sent away for a high school diploma.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, the opening line of his 1999 book Direct from Dell

blocks.text: Eight years old. Already trying to skip the middleman.

The plan failed, of course. He was too young, and he stayed in school like everyone else. But when he told the story decades later, he did not treat it as a cute joke. He treated it as the first sign of how his brain worked: "I've always been fascinated with eliminating unnecessary steps." __The idea that later built his company, cut out every step that does not help, first shows up in a child trying to skip nine years of school.__
A house that talked about money

Michael Saul Dell was born on ==23 February 1965== in Houston. His father, Alexander, was an orthodontist. His mother, Lorraine, became a stockbroker and financial consultant. He was the middle child, with one older brother and one younger brother.

His parents were not from Texas. In his 2021 memoir, Play Nice But Win, Dell writes that they moved from New York City to Houston in the 1960s because his father had heard the city was rich with opportunity. His father put his office in a building right next to the synagogue. Dell jokes that if you were Jewish and your teeth were crooked, there was a good chance his dad had fixed them. He also says his father became the city's top orthodontist mainly by outworking everyone else.

So this is not a rags-to-riches story, and you should know that up front. The family lived in an upper-middle-class part of west Houston. Dell himself says he worked as a child for a different reason: "I didn't actually have any need for income as a child, but I felt compelled to earn an income to fund my hobbies." He had a head start. What he did with it is the interesting part.
Not a poor kid. He worked because he wanted to.

His mother was the key. As Dell tells it, she was brilliant at maths and finance, and she became so good at investing in stocks and real estate that she turned it into a career as a stockbroker. Business and economics came up again and again at the family table. In a 2011 talk at the University of Texas, he described what an orthodontist father and a financial consultant mother meant in practice: a home full of conversation about money and science.
My parents were always talking about the economy and the stock market, and the oil crisis back in the '70s.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: For example: the magazines lying around the Dell home were Forbes, Fortune and Barron's, along with huge Value Line books full of pages of data on single companies. Dell says he soaked it all in. Texas Monthly adds one more detail about how early this started: at ==nine==, he got his own checkbook.

The family had a saying for when the brothers went out to play street ball with their friends: play nice, but win. Decades later, Dell used it as the title of his memoir. Soon his heroes were business people, above all the founders who challenged the way things were done and built something from nothing.
But all that business talk did not change what the family expected of him. Michael was supposed to become a doctor. He explained it in one flat sentence that many Indian students will know by heart.
My father's a doctor, my brother's a doctor, lots of doctors in the family, so I was going to be a doctor.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: Sound familiar? Hold on to this line. It comes back at Thanksgiving.
The kid who opened things

At home, he was the child who took things apart. Telephones, radios, televisions, whatever was electronic and within reach. "I liked to kind of see how it worked and sometimes I'd put them back together too," he says. Notice the word sometimes. He cared more about understanding the thing than about returning it in one piece.

One reference biography says he bought his first calculator at seven, with money from small jobs. He went to Herod Elementary School in Houston. The same biography calls him a top student there, but Dell remembers it differently: "I was an okay student." He says he did better in maths and science, and only when a subject interested him. He read science and science fiction, and he remembers reading Scientific American whenever it came.
An "okay student" by his own account. Keep that in mind.
Twelve years old, and busy

At ==12==, he got his first real job, as a dishwasher in a Chinese restaurant. He was promoted to water boy, and then to assistant maître d', the person who greets and seats guests. "So I was moving up pretty quickly in the Chinese restaurant business," he says, enjoying the joke. Then a Mexican restaurant recruited him away. He was 12 or 13, and employers were already competing for him.

That same stretch brought his first look at a computer. In seventh grade he was in an advanced maths class, and his teacher's room got the school's first teletype terminal. This was before personal computers. You typed a program, sent it off to a distant mainframe, and the answer came back. He was hooked, and he stayed after school to program it.

Then there was the ride home. His route on the bike took him past a RadioShack that sat between his junior high school and his house. Inside was a very simple personal computer. He would hang out in the store and wish that one day he could buy one. Every founder story has a moment like this, and it is usually smaller than you would expect.
My first encounter with a personal computer was riding my bike home from school.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: What can you take from these years? Not the money, because you cannot pick your parents. Take the habits instead, because those cost nothing. He asked how things worked, and he opened them to find out. He listened when adults talked about prices and the economy. And he kept looking for the step in any process that nobody actually needed.

It began with stamps. Around the age of 12, Michael was collecting them when he noticed that prices were rising. The usual way to sell was through an auction, with an auctioneer in the middle. So he asked a simple question. Why not go straight to the collectors?

So he built a ==12-page catalogue== of his own stamps and his friends' stamps, typing it himself with one finger. He got the names of people who took part in stamp show auctions and mailed the catalogue to them. He also bought an ad in a stamp collectors' magazine, under the name Dell's Stamps. Then the orders came in, and the money with them: ==$2,000==.

For example: he did not need to own every stamp a customer wanted. When orders came from collectors who wanted to skip the hassle of an auction, he went out and found the stamps afterwards. A Chicago Tribune writer spotted the link in 1999: this was the same order-first, build-later model people later met when they called Dell for a computer.
Order first, find the stamps after. Remember this when you reach the factory.

__He was cutting out the middleman before he was old enough to drive.__ This is why the stamp story matters more than the $2,000. A 12-year-old had found out two things. People will pay for skipping the hassle, and a seller who hears from the buyer first does not have to guess.
At 13: real money

Most 13-year-olds do not read commodity reports. Michael did. Living with a mother immersed in stocks and bonds, he became interested in currencies, interest rates and commodity prices. Then he began investing in stocks and precious metals using what he earned from his jobs.
Kind of an odd thing for a 13-year-old to be doing, but I found it interesting.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: The interviewer asked the question anyone would ask. Was this real money? "Yes," he said. Was his mother fine with that? "She was totally fine with that." Think about what that kind of trust does to a child's confidence.
At 14: the coin shop

His next job was at a stamp and coin store, at about ==14==. People walked in wanting to sell their rings or their silver. Michael's job was to assess the metal, work out what it was really worth, and then negotiate with them to buy it at a good price. Picture it for a second. A boy too young to drive is across the counter from an adult, bargaining over their silver.
Numbers, plus a real human on the other side. Priceless training.

There was a limit to all this, and it was transport. Until 16, he says, your only choices are a bicycle or asking your parents for a lift, which cut down the jobs he could take. Even so, he had now washed dishes, greeted guests, sold stamps by mail, traded metals and invested in markets. And he was not yet 16.
At 15: he breaks the Apple II

By now he had found Byte, a magazine about microcomputers and microprocessors. He subscribed, read each issue from cover to cover, and then read it again. One month it carried a piece by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak on the Apple II, and Michael decided he had to have one. After a lot of persuading, his parents let him spend his own savings. By his memoir's account, the bill came to almost ==$1,300==.

He collected the computer, brought it home, and took it apart immediately. His parents were furious. They had just watched their son pour his savings into a machine and then dismantle it on arrival. He had a reason, and he gives it in one line.
I wanted to see how it works, so I took it apart.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: It turned out to be a school in itself. Early personal computers used standard chips, so you could get a book on each chip and read what every pin did. You could design your own circuits and watch the signals move through them. "That was sort of the classroom for me," he says. Then came the better question: how could you make it do more, go faster, and talk to other computers?

He got it back together, and he used it. The Franklin Institute says he ran a bulletin board system on the machine, an early online message board, and he met other computer fans that way. He also began tutoring neighbourhood kids on how to get the most from their own Apple IIs. That paid well too, so now the hobby was paying for itself.

In 1980, he heard that Steve Jobs was coming to Houston to speak to his Apple user group. Jobs was just 25, and Michael had been reading about him in the business magazines with intense admiration. In his memoir, Dell says the room seemed to part when Jobs walked in, and that he spoke with passion about how personal computers would let people do what had seemed impossible. Michael was 15 years old and sitting in that room.
He studied founders the way other kids study cricketers.
At 16: the job that became a method

At ==16== he could finally drive, and he got a job with the Houston Post selling subscriptions over the phone. The job meant cold calls, and cold calls waste a lot of time. Michael did what he had always done, and looked for the pattern. He noticed that speaking the way a customer spoke helped. Then he noticed something better about the people who said yes.
Either they were moving to a new residence or they were getting married.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: A normal salesman might have shrugged and picked up the phone again. Michael asked where you could find those people in bulk. The answer was the courthouse. In Texas, a marriage licence application was public information, including the address where the licence should be sent. He hired all his friends, sent them across the ==16 counties== surrounding Houston, and had them copy down the addresses.

He then used his Apple II to produce the mailing, sending each couple a letter offering a free trial of the paper. He added people applying for mortgages too. In his memoir he says he also went to Houston's new apartment and condo blocks during a building boom, and offered their new residents two free weeks through a simple form. He was named salesman of the month. He sold thousands of subscriptions.

For example: a cold call asks a stranger to want a newspaper. A letter to a couple who just moved reaches them at the one moment they are actually building a new routine. Dell imitates that customer's thinking perfectly: "Oh, I got a new house. I'm nesting. Okay. The newspaper, that sounds like a good idea." Same product, same price, very different odds.

blocks.text: Then came the scene everyone remembers. His government economics teacher set the class an assignment: fill out a tax return. Michael filled in his own and turned it in. "Well this is obviously wrong," she told him. "No. I did the assignment. This is my tax return," he answered. Her reply: "Well this can't be right. You made more money than I did!"
He handed in his real tax return as homework.

She was upset, and he remembers that clearly. But the way he describes the whole episode is the part worth noting: "It was kind of like a big, big game for me." He does not think of himself as purely a salesman, either. He says the skill was looking at a problem from a different angle and not being afraid of a completely new thought. __Great selling, in his telling, starts as research.__ "It was data-driven," he says, and he later carried the same habit into Dell.
One warning: data rules are stricter now. Check the law before copying this.
At 16 and 17: what was inside the IBM

In 1981, IBM released its personal computer, and he bought one and did what he always did. He opened it. IBM was then the giant of American business, so what he found surprised him. Almost nothing inside was made by IBM. The parts came from other companies, so a clever kid could buy the same parts too.
The earliest PCs had IBM's name on the outside but there was no IBM on the inside.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: Next he did the arithmetic. A typical IBM PC sold for about $3,000, and the shop that sold it kept about $1,000 of that as gross profit. The parts inside cost around $700. He could also see the delay. He would read about a new technology in Byte, and then it would take a year or more before anyone could actually buy it. "So I was kind of a frustrated consumer," he says. That is usually how a good idea feels at the start.

blocks.text: In ==June 1982==, the National Computer Conference came to Houston. He was 17 and he skipped classes for most of a week to go. In his memoir he compares it to Disneyland, with booth after booth of peripherals, terminals and software. It was not the last time school lost out to computers. By his own account he sat at the back of his classes reading computer magazines.

The first customers came almost by accident. A lawyer, the father of a boy Michael was tutoring, heard about the machine he had souped up and asked for the same work on his own. He paid for the parts plus a fee. He then told other lawyers and doctors. When one doctor asked which PC he should buy for Michael to customise, Michael told him not to bother, and said he would buy it, upgrade it and sell it to him at a reasonable markup.
That is a computer business. He was still in high school.

He went to Memorial High School in Hedwig Village, which drew students from wealthy Houston neighbourhoods and offered competitive classes in computer science and economics. A 1991 Forbes article, quoted in a reference biography, recorded his goal in those years: to "make more money than any other kid in school." His senior year gave him a scene to match. He went to a BMW dealer with his parents, and when it came time to pay, the salesman looked to them.

Michael took out a cashier's check for ==$15,000==, then paid the rest with cash. That is how his memoir tells it, and other accounts agree that he bought the car with his own money as a teenager. We found no reliable record of him being bullied or in serious trouble at school. He simply kept finding better things to do than class. And still, the plan at home had not changed.
He paid cash. At seventeen.

blocks.text: By the summer of 1983, Michael Dell had most of what he would later need. He had a method for finding customers, a parts-and-prices map of the PC business, and real buyers. He applied to only one college, the University of Texas at Austin, where he would study to be a doctor. He packed his BMW and drove there with ==three personal computers== in the back seat.

blocks.text: In the fall of 1983, Michael Dell began at the University of Texas at Austin as a pre-med biology student. He really did mean to go. "I was going to school and had every intention of going to school," he says. He called the computer work a fun hobby, and one with a useful side effect: "it provided a little extra income, so I could buy the latest stereo and whatever I wanted to buy."

He lived in the Dobie Center, a private residential complex near the campus, in ==room 2713==. A hobby is a generous word for what happened there. He made and sold upgrade kits, adding hard disk drives and extra memory to the limited PCs of the day. His customers were students and local business people who found him by word of mouth. He bought computers, souped them up, and sold them on.
The dorm room sort of looked like a computer lab. There were soldering irons and all this stuff all over the place.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, speaking at the University of Texas, November 2011

photo.caption: The Dobie Center in Austin, seen in 2019. The business that became Dell started in one of its rooms.
photo.author: Michael Barera

blocks.text: Here is the part that shows how sharp he was. Some computer shops had IBM PCs they could not sell. Michael bought those unsold machines from them at cost, added memory and disk drives, and sold them for ==10 to 15 percent below retail==. The shop got rid of a problem, and his customer got a better machine for less. Everybody won, except the normal way of doing things.

For example: he applied for a vendor licence so he could bid on contracts from the State of Texas. A freshman in a dorm was now up against computer dealers, and he won bids. He had an advantage the dealers did not have, because he had no shop, no sales floor and almost no overhead.
No office was his advantage, not his weakness. Read this twice.

Not everyone around him enjoyed it. One reference biography, drawing on his own book, says his roommates grew so tired of the mess that they dumped his computer parts against the door and told him to move out. Dell does not hide that he was a poor college student during this time, either. He later put it plainly: "I wasn't very successful as a student, as far as that goes."
"Where are your books?"

The news reached Houston by the route such news always takes. His parents' friends told them, "Oh, Michael's doing so great. His business is going really well." His parents answered, "What are you talking about? He's supposed to be in college." So in ==November 1983== they made a couple of surprise visits to Austin.

He remembers the questioning. "Where are your books?" they asked. "Oh, they're at the library," he answered. The Academy of Achievement says that during one visit he rushed to hide his parts in a friend's room. It did not hold up for long. As he puts it, they finally figured out, "Wait a second. There's too many computer parts around here."
Every student who has hidden a side project knows this feeling.

Then came the talk. "Michael, you've got to get your priorities straight," they told him. His father asked what he wanted to do with his life. His answer, as he records in Direct from Dell, is one of the great teenage lines in business: "I want to compete with IBM!" He was 18. He was talking about the most successful company in America, from a dorm room.
Ten days

Around Thanksgiving of 1983, his parents got him to promise. No more computer business, and only his studies from now on. He actually tried. It lasted about ==ten days==, and those days without the work changed everything. He had time to notice how much he missed it.
So actually, my parents telling me to stop doing it is probably what caused the company to get created.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, Academy of Achievement interview, 2008

blocks.text: __A hobby you can drop is a hobby. A hobby you cannot drop is telling you something.__ That is what the ten days showed him. "I knew in my heart," he later wrote in his book, "that I was onto a fabulous business opportunity that I could not let pass me by." In 2011 he said it more simply, that the ban "probably threw me in even deeper."

What he did next is not something to copy without thinking. He did not tell them. "So like any other 18-year-old who wants to do what their parents don't want them to do, you just don't tell them," he says. He moved out of the dorm and into a bigger place at 32nd and Duval streets, which he chose because its high ceilings let him stack up stock. For a while, the secret held.
He kept it secret. It worked. It also could have blown up.

In ==January 1984== he registered the business as PC's Limited. He was 18, still weeks away from turning 19. The orders were growing fast by then, helped by small ads in computer magazines. By January he was filling about $30,000 of parts orders a month. By the end of the school year it was around $80,000 a month. About half the early business came from around Austin, and half from everywhere else.

blocks.text: The truth about the famous $1,000

You have probably heard that Dell started with $1,000. That is true, but the number has a funny origin. A customer who was a lawyer offered to incorporate the business in exchange for a hard-drive upgrade on his PC. Then Dell found out that Texas law required a company to have $1,000 to incorporate. __The famous figure was simply the legal minimum, and it was not a clever budget.__

He did not even have the cash sitting ready. According to the Austin American-Statesman's report of his 2011 talk, he had to sell a few more computers to raise the cash. The lawyer also hit a naming problem. "PC's Limited" was thought too generic for a corporate name, so he filed the papers as Dell Computer Corp., doing business as PC's Limited. So the Dell name went onto the legal papers because of a naming problem.
Even the most famous startup number has a boring explanation.

The timing was absurd. This all happened right before finals week in May 1984, and Dell admits it may not have been wise. "Maybe that wasn't such a good idea," he told CNBC, "but when you're 19 years old, you haven't developed all the skills you need in terms of judgement and rational thinking." That is a rare thing to hear from a founder. He is telling you that part of his courage was simply being young.
The deal

He still had to face his parents. By spring break, he told them the truth. Then he came to them with a proposal, and it was smart. He had checked with the university, and at UT you could take a semester off and come back. He would take off fall 1984 and try the business. If it worked, he would continue, and if not, he would go back to school.
It was a $1,000 investment, and if it didn't work, I would go right back to school.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, speaking at the University of Texas, November 2011

blocks.text: Look closely at what he did there. He did not ask his parents to believe in him. He asked them to compare a small, known cost with a large, unknown upside. "When I was 19 years old, the risk-reward was overwhelmingly in favor of taking the risk," he says. __He made quitting reversible, and that made it easy to say yes.__ That idea is useful for you too, because leaving a course is much less scary when you know the way back.

They agreed, though not happily. "My parents weren't really supportive," he told Forbes in 2011. In his 2008 interview he added an honest detail: "If they hadn't agreed, I probably would've done it anyway to be honest with you." In ==May 1984== he incorporated the company. He was 19, and the classroom was over for him.

blocks.text: Who actually shaped him

We looked for one wise mentor behind this teenager, and in these years there was not an obvious one. His influences were more scattered. His mother taught him how markets work. His father showed him what working harder than everyone looked like. Byte taught him the technology, Steve Jobs showed him a young founder in the flesh, and a lawyer's small upgrade job showed him that real customers existed.

Even his parents' objection counted, as he says himself. The force that pushed him hardest was the people telling him to stop. Asked later what young founders need, he said that no one can tell you how to do it, and that people who go looking for ideas to make money do worse than people who ask, "What do I really love to do?"

One small visitor gives us a last look at this moment. Soon after the move out of the dorm, a 25-year-old computer reseller from Dallas drove down to Austin to pick up hard drives for his own customers. He found a young founder in a little office and warehouse space, and he was impressed enough to write him a thank-you letter, predicting bigger things ahead. His name was Mark Cuban. "I was so impressed by this young kid," Cuban later wrote.
Future billionaire, writing fan mail to another future billionaire.

The fall semester of 1984 began without him. A pre-med student who had promised to give this up was now the owner of a real company, with a real name on the paperwork and a very small safety net. The doctor plan was over. Now he had to find out whether a teenager's idea could stand up against IBM.

Most founder stories show you the one thing that worked. This chapter shows every company, fund and big project we could trace to Michael Dell, including the ones his company would rather you forgot. We count ==26==. He truly founded only two of them himself: a computer company and a family investment firm. The rest he launched inside Dell, bought, backed, or fought over.
Count the failures as you read. There are more than you think.

blocks.name: PC's Limited, then Dell Computer, Dell Inc. and Dell Technologies
blocks.idea: Sell IBM-compatible PCs straight to the people using them, through magazine ads and a phone line, and build each one after the order comes in. Cutting out the dealer removed a markup of 10 to 15 percent. In 1985 his Turbo PC sold for $795, well under IBM's price.
blocks.decision: Dealers would not stock an unknown teenager's machines, so he went around them and made that the whole strategy. The early turning points were bringing in 44-year-old investment banker Lee Walker as president in 1986, and dropping the name PC's Limited for Dell Computer in 1987.
blocks.howStarted: From a dorm room to a condominium to a 1,000-square-foot office. By 1986 the company had 100 workers, and then a factory of more than 80,000 square feet in north Austin was turning out 7,000 machines a month. Early buyers were computer-savvy individuals and nearby businesses, and big companies and government agencies followed.
blocks.funding: $1,000 to incorporate. Then the part the legend skips: a Harvard Business School case says his family lent the firm $500,000, repaid by the end of 1986. After that came bank loans including a $10 million credit line, more than $21 million in a 1987 private placement, and a stock market listing in 1988.
blocks.whatHappened: Sales went from $6 million in 1985 to $159 million in 1988 and $25.3 billion in 2000. It became the world's top computer seller in 2001, lost that spot to HP in 2006, went private in 2013 and came back to the stock market in 2018. Revenue in the year to January 2026 was a record $113.5 billion.
blocks.lesson: If the gatekeeper will not let you in, ask whether you need the gatekeeper at all. His weakness, no dealers, became his edge.

blocks.text: A $500,000 family loan. The $1,000 legend has a footnote.

Look again at that funding line, because it changes how the story reads. The famous $1,000 is real, and it was what the company was incorporated with. But the Harvard case, citing a published profile of him, says his family also lent the firm ==$500,000== for its early operations. So this was a brilliant idea and a real risk, and it also had a family safety net. __Most "self-made" stories have a line like this somewhere, so go looking for it before you compare yourself to anyone.__

blocks.name: Olympic
blocks.idea: A single family of machines to cover desktops, workstations and servers, with one or two processors and many operating systems. Dell later called it a "boil the ocean" product, which means trying to do everything at once.
blocks.decision: The company was doing about $250 million a year and wanted a product that would put it on the map. It had just hired computer scientist Glenn Henry from IBM, and he built research and development up from almost nothing to 150 engineers. The safer option was to keep making small improvements to what already sold.
blocks.howStarted: An internal project with a large group of young engineers. It went in front of the public as prototypes at the Comdex trade show in November 1989.
blocks.funding: Company money. Dell's research budget was only about $7 million in 1989, and Olympic took perhaps half of it.
blocks.whatHappened: Customers said no. "Thanks very much, but we don't need that much technology," is how Dell recalls the verdict. He shut it before any product shipped, kept the engineers, and reused the graphics and disk technology in a broad new product line within six to nine months.
blocks.lesson: Show your idea to paying customers before you fall in love with it. And when you kill a project, keep the people.

blocks.name: Selling through shops: the first retail experiment
blocks.idea: Reach small businesses and home buyers who wanted to see a computer before paying, through CompUSA, Staples, Best Buy, Sam's Club and others.
blocks.decision: Conventional wisdom said direct selling would only ever be a niche, and Dell gave in to it. The alternative, which he later went back to, was to stay direct and keep the customer relationship for himself.
blocks.howStarted: A 1990 deal with Soft Warehouse superstores, later renamed CompUSA, at mail-order prices, followed by Staples in 1991.
blocks.funding: No special funding. The real cost was hidden: when Dell cut prices, it had to pay stores for the fall in value of machines sitting on their shelves.
blocks.whatHappened: It helped push sales from $890 million to over $2 billion. But when Dell finally measured profit by channel, retail was about 10 percent of sales and lost money. "We were losing our shirts," CFO Tom Meredith told Fortune. Dell walked out in 1994.
blocks.lesson: Count profit per channel, not just sales. A channel can grow every month and still be killing you.

blocks.name: The first notebook line
blocks.idea: Get into the fastest-growing part of the PC market: laptops. Dell's first notebook arrived in 1991 and a colour model followed in 1992.
blocks.decision: By 1993 the machines had quality problems. New hire John Medica, who had been chief designer of Apple's PowerBook, persuaded Dell to scrap every existing laptop plan and bet on one premium model. The other choice was to keep patching a bad line.
blocks.howStarted: Medica's redo took an extra six months of customer research before the design was settled.
blocks.funding: Dell's own money, and a $20 million write-off for the cancelled models.
blocks.whatHappened: Dell sat out the market for more than a year. Notebooks fell from 12 percent of its system revenue to 3 percent. Then the Latitude XP launched in August 1994 and sold about 34,000 units in one quarter, as many as all of Dell's 1993 laptops combined.
blocks.lesson: Sometimes starting over is cheaper than fixing. Hire the person who built your rival's best product and then actually listen to them.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern already. Each of these failures happened when Dell stopped doing the thing that made it different, or stopped listening to the buyer. And each failure handed him a rule he used for decades. Olympic gave him "relevant technology". The retail exit gave him total focus on direct sales. The notebook mess gave him a reason to hire people who knew more than he did.

blocks.name: Dell.com
blocks.idea: Take the phone-order model online: let buyers configure a PC, see the price, order it and track it.
blocks.decision: After leaving shops in 1994, Dell needed a new way to grow. It tested kiosks and online shopping services first, and the web won.
blocks.howStarted: A site offering technical support and product information came first, and online shopping for PCs followed in 1996, aimed mainly at catalogue customers. Big clients got private "Premier Pages".
blocks.funding: Paid for by the business itself. No outside money.
blocks.whatHappened: Sales through the site passed $1 million a day in 1996, $12 million a day in 1998 and about $50 million a day by 2000. By mid-2000 there were over 50,000 Premier Pages.
blocks.lesson: New technology pays best when it speeds up something you already do well.

blocks.name: MSD Capital, now DFO Management
blocks.idea: A private firm to invest his personal fortune outside Dell. MSD stands for his initials, Michael Saul Dell.
blocks.decision: Almost everything he owned was one tech stock. He chose diversification, and hired two professional investors, Glenn Fuhrman and John Phelan, rather than picking stocks himself.
blocks.howStarted: An office in New York, far from Texas. The Wall Street Journal reported in December 1998 that he had quietly launched it.
blocks.funding: His own money. The Journal reported "resources of $1 billion" in 1998, and a later 2019 article put the start at $400 million.
blocks.whatHappened: By 2013 it held an estimated $16 billion across stocks, companies, real estate and timberland, including businesses in dentistry and landscaping. It paid $875 million for the Boca Raton resort in 2019 and owns about 7.5 percent of the developer Related. It was restructured as DFO Management at the end of 2022.
blocks.lesson: Your company is your biggest risk as well as your biggest asset. Move some winnings away from it, and hire professionals to do it.

blocks.name: A first cheque to Silver Lake
blocks.idea: Back a new private equity firm that invested only in technology, run by people he already knew.
blocks.decision: He had met co-founder Roger McNamee on his IPO road show in the late 1980s, and knew the other founders too. One of MSD's first investments went into Silver Lake's first fund.
blocks.howStarted: A cheque into an unknown fund, followed by years of staying in touch, including vacation homes in the same Hawaiian community as several partners.
blocks.funding: MSD's money. The amount is not public.
blocks.whatHappened: More than a decade later, Silver Lake's Egon Durban became his partner in the 2013 buyout, then in EMC. Silver Lake also held about 10 percent of VMware when Broadcom bought it, a stake CRN said could bring it about $6 billion.
blocks.lesson: Stay close to smart people long before you need anything from them. That small early cheque later helped make the biggest deals of his life possible.

blocks.name: Dell Ventures
blocks.idea: A company fund to buy stakes in internet start-ups, for financial gains and early looks at new technology.
blocks.decision: Everyone in tech was doing it, and Dell had the cash. Its later head described the first version as late-stage investing that used Dell's balance sheet to chase capital gains.
blocks.howStarted: Set up in 1999 inside Dell. By July 2000 it had put about $700 million into roughly 50 internet companies.
blocks.funding: Dell's own balance sheet.
blocks.whatHappened: When the Nasdaq collapsed, Dell said its investment portfolio was down more than $1 billion. It chose to sell the portfolio and wound the effort down in 2004. A much smaller, strategy-led Dell fund restarted around 2012. After the EMC merger, EMC's own venture team became Dell Technologies Capital. That team led the first institutional round of the security firm Zscaler in 2012, and says it has invested more than $1.8 billion since.
blocks.lesson: Do not invest because everyone else is. The second version worked because it had a reason besides greed.

blocks.name: The dot-com side shows: Gigabuys, Dellnet, DellHost, Dell Auctions, Dell Marketplace
blocks.idea: Use Dell's famous website to sell everything else: 30,000 electronics products on Gigabuys.com, internet access through Dellnet, web hosting through DellHost, used PCs through Dell Auctions, and a business-to-business exchange called Dell Marketplace.
blocks.decision: The core PC business was showing signs of slowing and the internet hype was at its peak. Dell even risked competing with its own customers by entering web hosting. Compaq publicly refused to do the same.
blocks.howStarted: Gigabuys in March 1999. DellHost in February 2000 through a partner, Interliant. Dell Marketplace in autumn 2000 with software partner Ariba.
blocks.funding: Dell's own cash. We found no public figures for each one.
blocks.whatHappened: Dell Marketplace closed in February 2001 after only three suppliers signed up. Press reported in August 2001 that Dell was pulling out of hosting through a deal with Sprint, and that Marketplace and Auctions were already gone. We could not find a reliable closing date for Gigabuys or Dellnet.
blocks.lesson: Being great at selling your own product does not make you great at running a marketplace for everyone else's.

blocks.text: Even winners catch the fever. Dell chased hype too, and paid for it.

blocks.name: The consumer push: Axim, Dell DJ, Dell Music Store, TVs and printers
blocks.idea: Treat gadgets like PCs: use Dell's low-cost model to crush prices in handhelds, music players, printers and flat-screen TVs. It was a bet on the "digital home" with the PC at its centre.
blocks.decision: Dell earned most of its money from businesses and wanted another engine of growth. A marketing vice-president told TIME they were laying "the foundation for trench warfare". Some doubters inside the company asked whether customers would really buy ink online.
blocks.howStarted: The Axim handheld launched in November 2002 at $199, against rivals at $400 to $600, and quickly took nearly 38 percent of its US market. Printers followed in March 2003, and the Digital Jukebox, music store and TVs were announced that September.
blocks.funding: Dell's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: The music player never threatened the iPod. Dell dropped the hard-drive DJ in early 2006 and the $99 DJ Ditty on 17 August 2006, less than a year after launch. It stopped selling the Axim in April 2007 as handhelds shrank. Fortune said in 2005 that consumer electronics had proved harder than expected.
blocks.lesson: Low prices win when buyers are comparing specifications. They lose when buyers want a product they love.

blocks.name: Dell Direct kiosks
blocks.idea: Small mall stands where people could touch a Dell, then order it for delivery. They carried no stock, so they fitted the direct model.
blocks.decision: Consumers wanted to see machines, but Dell did not want to go back to selling through shops.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 2002 in US shopping malls, staffed by Dell representatives.
blocks.funding: Dell's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: There were more than 140 in the US by 2008. Dell shut them all on 30 January 2008, once its products were on sale in over 10,000 retail outlets worldwide. Dell said the need for them had declined.
blocks.lesson: A half-step can be a useful experiment. Know when it has finished teaching you.

blocks.name: Alienware
blocks.idea: Buy a cult gaming-PC maker with UFO-themed machines costing an average of $3,000 to $4,000.
blocks.decision: Dell already had its own high-end XPS line, but no credibility with gamers and little chance of creating it. The deal, rumoured for weeks, was announced in March 2006. Forbes noted it was only Dell's third acquisition ever.
blocks.howStarted: Founded in Miami in 1996 by childhood friends Nelson Gonzalez and Alex Aguila. Dell left it as a separate subsidiary with its own brand, design, marketing and support, and said none of about 700 staff were expected to be laid off.
blocks.funding: A Dell purchase on undisclosed terms.
blocks.whatHappened: Alienware got Dell's supply chain, cutting wait times that had run four to six weeks. Dell got a credible gaming brand. It also brought in machines using AMD chips, which Dell had resisted selling until then. That matters later in this book.
blocks.lesson: If you cannot build a reputation, buy it, and then do not smother it.

blocks.text: By 2007, Dell's PC business was under attack, and his answer was to go shopping. From 2010 to 2012 alone, the company spent about ==$14 billion== on eleven businesses, trying to become a seller of software, services and data-centre gear to large companies. The next six ventures are the pieces of that plan. Some became gold, and some were sold at a loss.

blocks.name: EqualLogic
blocks.idea: Buy a maker of networked storage for mid-sized companies, so Dell would own its storage technology instead of reselling others'.
blocks.decision: Michael Dell returned as CEO in 2007, and this was his opening move into big-company technology.
blocks.howStarted: Dell agreed to buy it in 2007 and kept the brand and its reseller network, even though Dell had built its name on avoiding resellers.
blocks.funding: $1.4 billion in cash, by far Dell's largest deal at that point.
blocks.whatHappened: The deal closed in January 2008. CRN later said it set the foundation for Dell's reseller partner programme.
blocks.lesson: One purchase can force you to change a belief. Dell bought storage and also bought its way back into reselling.

blocks.name: Perot Systems, renamed Dell Services
blocks.idea: Buy an IT services and outsourcing company, founded by Texas billionaire Ross Perot, so Dell could sell advice and long contracts as well as boxes.
blocks.decision: Rivals IBM and HP were already big in services. Texas Monthly called this a "me-too" move. Dell paid $30 a share.
blocks.howStarted: An existing company, added to Dell's other purchases.
blocks.funding: About $3.9 billion, paid by Dell.
blocks.whatHappened: In March 2016, needing cash for the EMC deal, Dell agreed to sell it to Japan's NTT Data for $3.06 billion. Ars Technica's headline counted the loss at about $800 million.
blocks.lesson: A deal that looks strategic can still lose money. Copying your rivals' move late usually costs you a premium.

blocks.name: 3PAR: the deal that got away
blocks.idea: Buy a high-end storage maker to fill the top of Dell's storage range.
blocks.decision: Dell agreed to $18 a share, $1.15 billion, on 16 August 2010, an 87 percent premium. HP jumped in at $24. The two raised their bids in public for about two weeks. Dell reached $32, then chose to stop.
blocks.howStarted: Dell made the first agreed offer, on terms that included a break-up fee.
blocks.funding: Dell's cash, had it won.
blocks.whatHappened: HP won at $33 a share, or $2.35 billion, about ten times 3PAR's yearly revenue. 3PAR paid Dell a $72 million break-up fee. Dell later bought another storage firm, Compellent, for about $938 million.
blocks.lesson: Decide your walk-away price before the auction starts. Losing cleanly can be better than winning badly.

blocks.name: Boomi
blocks.idea: A small cloud service that moves data between a company's different software systems. Salesforce was a client.
blocks.decision: Cloud software was the new growth area, and IBM had just bought a similar company. Dell had just lost 3PAR.
blocks.howStarted: Founded in Pennsylvania in 2000. It had raised $4 million in its first institutional round in 2008.
blocks.funding: A Dell purchase on undisclosed terms.
blocks.whatHappened: By 2021 it had more than 15,000 customers. Dell sold it to Francisco Partners and TPG for about $4 billion in cash, and the filing shows a $4.0 billion pre-tax gain on the sale.
blocks.lesson: Your smallest, cheapest purchase may turn out to be the best. Boomi was a footnote in 2010 and a $4 billion cheque in 2021.

blocks.name: Dell Software: Quest and SonicWall
blocks.idea: Create a software arm by buying IT-management tools from Quest and network security from SonicWall.
blocks.decision: Dell named John Swainson as software chief in March 2012 with a mandate to expand. Software was meant to lift profit margins.
blocks.howStarted: Bought from existing owners: SonicWall in spring 2012 and Quest later that year.
blocks.funding: Dell's cash: about $1.2 billion for SonicWall, as reported, since Dell kept that price private, and $2.4 billion for Quest.
blocks.whatHappened: In June 2016, Dell sold the software group to Francisco Partners and Elliott Management, reportedly for just over $2 billion. That is well under the $3.6 billion it had paid for those two alone. Elliott was the same activist fund that had pushed EMC toward a sale.
blocks.lesson: When you need cash for a bigger bet, your old bets go on sale. Being willing to take that loss is part of betting big.

blocks.name: SecureWorks
blocks.idea: A security-services firm that watches corporate networks for attacks. At purchase it protected over 3,000 customers, including more than 1,500 banks and credit unions.
blocks.decision: Dell wanted security inside its services offer to large companies.
blocks.howStarted: Bought for about $612 million, closing in February 2011.
blocks.funding: Dell's cash. Its 2016 stock market listing raised $112 million at $14 a share, while Dell's parent kept about 86.8 percent of the shares.
blocks.whatHappened: Sophos bought the company in February 2025 for $8.50 a share, about $859 million in total. Michael Dell had chaired its board since 2015.
blocks.lesson: A stock listing does not prove a business is winning. This one sold for about 40 percent below its listing price nine years later.

blocks.name: Phones, tablets and Adamo
blocks.idea: Compete with Apple and Android makers using Dell-built phones and tablets, plus a thin luxury laptop called Adamo at $2,000.
blocks.decision: The world was going mobile and Dell had nothing to sell. It entered late, and Dell's own statements kept pointing to future products.
blocks.howStarted: A phone with China Mobile in 2009. In the US, the Aero phone and 5-inch Streak arrived in August 2010, then the Venue and Venue Pro.
blocks.funding: Dell's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: The Streak 5 died after about a year, and the Streak 7 in December 2011. Adamo ended in 2011. In March 2012, Dell stopped selling smartphones in the US, while the Venue Pro kept selling in India. A Dell vice-president declared that year: "We're no longer a PC company."
blocks.lesson: A me-too product with no one behind it dies quietly. Enter a market with real commitment or do not enter.

blocks.text: So by 2012 the scoreboard looked bad. Billions had gone into acquisitions, the consumer gadgets had flopped, and investors still treated Dell as a dying PC maker. What came next was three giant deals in a row. __Each of those deals was mostly other people's money, and each one depended on him being willing to put his own name and fortune on the line.__
Next: the biggest bets. The full story is in the following chapters.

blocks.name: The 2013 buyout (Denali Holding)
blocks.idea: Buy Dell back from public shareholders and rebuild it without quarterly pressure.
blocks.decision: Investor Southeastern and then Silver Lake raised the idea in 2012. KKR, TPG and Blackstone looked and walked away, citing PC risk. HP never bid.
blocks.howStarted: Conversations in Hawaii in August 2012 with his neighbour Egon Durban. Michael Dell told the board first and a committee of independent directors ran the sale.
blocks.funding: About $24.9 billion in total at the final price. His own shares, worth about $3.7 billion, plus $750 million cash from him and an affiliate, about $1.4 billion from Silver Lake, a $2 billion Microsoft loan, and new debt.
blocks.whatHappened: After a public fight with Carl Icahn, shareholders approved it on 12 September 2013, and he ended up with 74.9 percent. Dell returned to the stock market in December 2018.
blocks.lesson: When the market hates your stock and you believe in the business, cheap shares are an opportunity. So are the lawsuits that come with it.

blocks.name: EMC
blocks.idea: Buy the world's leading data-storage maker, with its 81 percent stake in the software company VMware, and become a one-stop shop for corporate technology.
blocks.decision: Rivals such as HP were shedding businesses. Dell went the other way. He had looked at EMC in 2009 and the talks failed. EMC was under pressure from activist fund Elliott and its CEO was close to retiring.
blocks.howStarted: A phone call to EMC's Joe Tucci less than a year after going private. Plans date to October 2014, and the deal was announced on 12 October 2015.
blocks.funding: About $67 billion: nearly $50 billion of debt, a new "tracking stock" tied to VMware, and new equity from Michael Dell, MSD Partners, Silver Lake and Singapore's Temasek.
blocks.whatHappened: It closed on 7 September 2016 with 98 percent of votes cast in favour, the biggest pure tech deal in history at the time. The new Dell Technologies carried nearly $57 billion of debt and paid down billions quickly.
blocks.lesson: When rivals shrink, ask whether being bigger could be your edge. But size only works if your cash flow can carry the debt.

blocks.name: VMware
blocks.idea: A software company that lets one computer behave like many. It came with EMC and was the real prize of the deal, growing at 10 percent a year.
blocks.decision: Selling it would have wiped out much debt at once. Dell and Durban kept it, used it as collateral, and took dividends from it instead.
blocks.howStarted: Already a listed company with its own board, and Michael Dell became chairman in 2016.
blocks.funding: Part of the EMC purchase. The tracking stock let public investors follow about half of Dell's VMware stake.
blocks.whatHappened: An $11 billion dividend helped fund the 2018 return to the market. An $11.5 billion dividend came with the spin-off to shareholders on 1 November 2021. Broadcom then agreed to buy it for $61 billion plus $8 billion of debt, closing in November 2023. Michael Dell personally owned about 40 percent.
blocks.lesson: Look for the asset in a deal that the market is undervaluing. Sometimes the hidden piece pays for the whole thing.

blocks.name: Pivotal
blocks.idea: A software-tools company carved out of EMC and VMware in 2013, with General Electric buying about 10 percent.
blocks.decision: It came with EMC, and Dell chose to take it public rather than fold it in.
blocks.howStarted: Listed on the New York Stock Exchange in April 2018 at $15 a share, raising $555 million. Dell kept about 70 percent of the shares.
blocks.funding: $1.7 billion from investors before the listing, including $182 million from Ford, as TechCrunch reported.
blocks.whatHappened: The stock fell from a high of $21.44 to $8.30 in a few months of 2019. VMware, also controlled by Dell, then bought it at an enterprise value of $2.7 billion. Public shareholders got $15 a share, the same price as the listing.
blocks.lesson: Hot stock market stories fade fast when growth slows. It helps if a big sibling can catch you, but don't plan on that.

blocks.name: RSA and other EMC pieces
blocks.idea: Use EMC's non-core businesses as a source of cash. RSA was a well-known security firm, and EMC's document-management unit was another.
blocks.decision: The debt forced the choice. Five days after the merger closed, the document unit went to OpenText.
blocks.howStarted: Inherited from EMC, which had paid just under $2.1 billion for RSA in 2006.
blocks.funding: None needed. These sales raised money.
blocks.whatHappened: OpenText paid $1.62 billion. RSA went to a Symphony Technology Group consortium for $2.075 billion in 2020, roughly what EMC had paid 14 years earlier.
blocks.lesson: Before a huge deal, list exactly what you would sell to pay for it. Dell's plan needed more than $6 billion of asset sales.

blocks.name: MSD Partners, now part of BDT & MSD Partners
blocks.idea: Open the family investing team's methods to outside rich families and institutions.
blocks.decision: MSD's record attracted other wealthy people, so in 2009 its leaders formed a separate firm that could take outside money.
blocks.howStarted: From MSD Capital's team and strategies, in New York, Santa Monica and West Palm Beach.
blocks.funding: Dell family capital first, then outside investors. It managed over $20 billion by 2022.
blocks.whatHappened: It merged in January 2023 with BDT & Company, the merchant bank of Byron Trott, known as Warren Buffett's investment banker, with about $50 billion in assets combined. Trott and Gregg Lemkau became co-CEOs, and Michael Dell chairs the advisory board.
blocks.lesson: A skill you build to solve your own problem can become a business for others.

blocks.name: AI servers
blocks.idea: Build the racks of Nvidia-powered servers that train and run AI models, and sell them with installation, support and financing.
blocks.decision: Dell launched its network server line in 1996 and already had the supply chain and customer list needed. It accepted thin profits on this work: its target is a mid-single-digit operating margin.
blocks.howStarted: Publicly visible from June 2024, when Michael Dell posted that Dell was building an "AI factory" with Nvidia for Elon Musk's xAI. CoreWeave expanded its relationship with Dell that December.
blocks.funding: Dell's own cash flow. Dell also offers its customers financing through its finance arm.
blocks.whatHappened: AI orders hit $64.1 billion in the year to January 2026. In the quarter reported on 1 September 2026, orders were a record $60.9 billion, with a backlog of $95 billion waiting to be delivered. Dell expects about $74 billion of AI server revenue that year.
blocks.lesson: Forty years of boring supply-chain skill became priceless when the whole world wanted the same scarce machines.

blocks.text: Add it up and an uncomfortable truth appears. Of these 26 bets, the ones that made him richest were not the ones he invented in a burst of genius. They were direct selling, a patient family office, and three huge deals built on cheap prices and other people's debt. __Failures were common, but none of them was big enough to end the game, and that is the part to copy.__

The third week of October 1987 should have killed the deal. Dell had hired Goldman Sachs and was raising money through a private placement, which means selling shares quietly to a small group of big investors rather than to the public. On ==19 October==, known as Black Monday, the US stock market lost more than a fifth of its value in one day. In his memoir, as read aloud on a podcast, Dell says his president Lee Walker came into his office convinced the deal was finished. He says he was busy taking apart a competitor's computer.

The deal survived. Dell claims it was the only one of hundreds of financings under way that day to make it through, and we could only check that claim against his own account. What the Harvard case confirms is that the placement closed in the wake of the crash and raised more than ==$21 million==. Investors were looking at a company doubling every year. __Numbers that strong can get a deal through a panic that scares everyone else away.__
Market crashing? He was opening a rival's PC. Focus is a superpower.

Next came the IPO. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a company first sells its shares to the public on a stock exchange. In ==June 1988==, Dell sold shares at $8.50 each, raising about $30 million and valuing the whole company at about $85 million. He was 23, and he still owned more than half of the company. He now had a public share price, public critics and a quarterly report card.

Around then he also showed how badly a young founder can handle experienced people. Dell had hired a group of marketing executives from Tandy, a bigger PC maker, and they quickly lifted gross margins from 23 to 31 percent. Then came fights over ad budgets and the size of the sales force. By early 1988 most of the Tandy group had resigned or been forced out. Some people at the time questioned whether he could share control at all.
Break one: the warehouse

The IPO cash was gone fast. Dell spent it on factory capacity and warehouse space, because it had been struggling to meet demand. Then it overestimated demand in the last quarter of 1988, and suddenly had no cash and warehouses full of unsold computers. For a company built on making machines only after an order came in, this was an embarrassing place to end up. It had also announced a clone of IBM's new PS/2 machine long before it was ready, and then could not deliver it on time.
Break two: the memory chips

In 1989 he made the mistake he still talks about. The industry was moving from one type of memory chip to a newer one, and Dell had loaded up on the older kind and designed its products around them. It was left holding chips it could not use or easily sell, and it had to raise prices to cover the loss. Add the Olympic write-off and the result was brutal: profits fell 65 percent to ==$5 million==, even though sales had doubled.
Failure is always an ingredient of success.

blocks.text: This is where the famous Dell supply chain really came from. In his own words, it grew out of "a horrible mistake we made in managing our supply chain", one that nearly took the company out of business. After that, Dell asked suppliers to hold parts close by and deliver them only when needed. __The thing he is most praised for began as a scar.__

For example: Dell later explained the maths of stock with a single sum. A typical rival held about 30 days of stock, plus another 40 days sitting with dealers. Dell held 12. That is a 58-day gap, and in 58 days, Dell said, parts prices fall about 6 percent. So on every machine, Dell paid the newer, lower price and its rival paid the older, higher one.
Very important for hardware founders. Stock loses value every single day.
Break three: the summer of 1993

Then growth nearly finished the job. "We went right from 890 million to 2.1 billion in one year," Dell remembers. "And everything started to fall apart." The company did not have the systems, the people or the capital for that size. Worse, much of that growth came through retail stores, where it was making no money.

The attacks came from outside too. On 20 November 1992, Kidder Peabody analyst David Korus questioned how Dell accounted for its currency trading, and suggested it might be flattering profits. Dell's officials heatedly denied that, and the stock fell $3.75 in a day. Dell itself went to the Securities and Exchange Commission about unusual trading in its shares. In February 1993, it withdrew a planned sale of four million shares, and its stock dropped nearly 17 percent in a day.

By August 1993 the numbers were out: a net loss of ==$75.7 million== in one quarter, its first since going public. The chief financial officer had resigned. Every new notebook line was scrapped. The stock had fallen from $49 in January to $16 by July. By November, short sellers held about 30 percent of the shares in public hands. A short seller borrows shares and sells them, betting that the price will fall so they can buy them back cheaper.
I felt a gradual panicking.

blocks.text: He had a harder time at night than the numbers show. "It's hard to not think about all the people you're responsible for," he told Tim Ferriss, thinking of employees who had moved their families to Austin. He was 28. And he has admitted the real danger: "we were running out of capital".
The airport

The turning point is a scene in Heathrow Airport. Dell was hurrying through it with Tom Meredith, his new chief financial officer from Sun Microsystems, to catch a plane to Ireland. Meredith said he saw a silver lining in the notebook disaster, because of what it had revealed about the company's information systems. Dell had not yet been breaking down profit by business segment, and it was time to look. Meredith's message was simple: growth had to be balanced with cash in the bank and real profit.
Any one strength used to excess becomes a weakness.
blocks.who: Tom Meredith, Dell CFO

blocks.text: Then Dell did something few 28-year-old founders manage: he went and got adults. With help from his board and a search firm, he recruited Mort Topfer, a 23-year Motorola veteran, as vice chairman. Fortune's headline two years later put it bluntly, saying a bunch of old guys got Michael Dell to grow up. __He gave up authority to keep the company, the opposite of what happened with the Tandy team a few years earlier.__

The cure was boring. Dell left retail. It began tracking cash and return on invested capital, and tied the pay of its top 500 managers to those numbers. It also leaned into a lovely quirk of direct selling: customers often paid Dell before Dell paid its suppliers, so growth could produce cash instead of eating it. In 1995, profits came in at ==$149 million== after the 1994 loss of $36 million.

What followed was one of the great runs in stock market history. Dell Computer was the best-performing American stock of the 1990s, up ==87,000 percent== by one Harvard count. Austin was never the same. At one point Dell's stock was said to have created 2,700 millionaires, nicknamed "Dellionaires", including secretaries. In 1991, Michael Dell was worth $300 million. By the end of the decade he was worth over $21 billion, the richest American under 40.

blocks.text: How he beat Compaq

His main early rival was Compaq, a fellow Texan that built expensive, high-quality machines. In the early 1990s, Compaq fought back with a PC at just $899, and Dell slashed prices by up to $1,400 to keep its share. Dell could do this because its operating costs were 18 percent of revenue, against Compaq's 36 percent. Compaq also sued Dell over its advertising and eventually won. But in a price war, the company with the lowest costs can stay in longest.

For example: when the world PC market had its worst slump yet in 2000 and 2001, most makers cut back. Dell started a price war. Rivals were slow to respond, and by 2001 Dell was number one in the world with a 13 percent share. It also made its first big layoffs, cutting 5,700 jobs, while still earning $1.78 billion.

Compaq's end shows how hard this market was. It disappeared into HP in 2002, and the merged giant took the top spot for a while before Dell got it back. Selling the most PCs turned out to be a dangerous prize, and __a lead built only on low cost lasts until someone else lowers their costs.__
Steve Jobs at the door

Here is a strange secret from this era, which Dell told only in 2021. In 1993, Steve Jobs visited Dell's house in Texas several times trying to sell him on the NeXT operating system. Dell said no, because there was too little software and too little customer interest. In 1997, back at Apple, Jobs tried again and showed him a Dell desktop running Mac OS. "Why don't you license the Mac OS?" Jobs asked, in Dell's telling.

Dell was interested and offered a licence fee on every PC sold with Mac OS. Jobs worried that this would eat into Mac sales, so he countered: put Mac OS and Windows on every Dell, and pay Apple on all of them. Dell refused to pay Apple for customers who used only Windows. That October he also gave one of the most famous bad answers in tech history.
What would I do? I'd shut it down and give the money back to the shareholders.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, asked in October 1997 what he would do with Apple

blocks.text: In January 2006, Apple's market value passed Dell's, $72.13 billion to $71.97 billion. Market value means the share price times all the shares, and it is the market's price tag for the whole company. Dell later said the line was misunderstood: he had first declined the question, and meant only that he could not imagine running any company but his own. He says the two stayed friends.
Never mock a rival in public. Apple's market value passed Dell's in 2006.
Intel's secret money

In July 2004 he handed the CEO job to Kevin Rollins, who had shared an office with him in a "two-in-a-box" arrangement, and stayed on as chairman. Under the surface, a problem had been growing. The Securities and Exchange Commission later alleged that Intel was paying Dell large sums not to use chips from its rival AMD. By the SEC's count, those payments rose from 10 percent of Dell's operating income in fiscal 2003 to 38 percent in fiscal 2006, and peaked at ==76 percent== in one quarter of fiscal 2007.

The SEC alleged that investors were not told, and that these payments, rather than management and operations, let Dell meet Wall Street's targets. Without them, it said, Dell would have missed its earnings target in every quarter from fiscal 2002 to 2006. When Dell added AMD, Intel cut the payments and profits sank. The SEC said executives then blamed pricing and component costs when speaking to investors.
for 3 qtrs now, Intel money has made the qtr. A bad way to run the railroad.
blocks.who: Kevin Rollins, internal email to Michael Dell, 2004, quoted by the SEC

blocks.text: In July 2010 it was settled. The company paid a ==$100 million== penalty, and Michael Dell and Rollins paid $4 million each, without admitting or denying the charges. The details matter: Dell's own statement says Michael Dell's settlement covered disclosure about Intel only, not the separate accounting fraud charges, and only claims that do not require fraudulent intent. He accepted a court order against future violations and stayed as CEO, with no restrictions on serving.
Ask where your profit really comes from. Then tell your investors the truth.
The bad years

Everything went wrong together. In October 2005, Dell warned of weak sales and took a charge of about $450 million, largely over faulty capacitors in desktops. At least 11.8 million computers made from 2003 to 2005 were at risk of failing, and one customer's lawsuit accused Dell of hiding the defects. Dell disputed that and settled in September 2010 on undisclosed terms. Meanwhile, customers were waiting 30 minutes to reach a support agent on the phone.

In August 2006 came the recall of about ==4.1 million== laptop batteries with Sony-made cells, because they could overheat. The US safety regulator called it the largest electronics recall it had handled. That same quarter, HP passed Dell as the world's biggest PC seller, by 16.3 percent to 16.1 percent in Gartner's count. By the end of the year it was not close, with HP at 17 to 18 percent and Dell at 14 to 15.

On 31 January 2007, Rollins left and Michael Dell took the CEO job back. Two days later he wrote to staff that results were "disappointing" and "unacceptable", and named a new foe: "bureaucracy, which costs us money and slows us down." He cut the number of managers reporting to him, and ended that year's bonuses. Then he did something harder, and began taking apart his own creed.
The direct model has been a revolution, but is not a religion.
blocks.who: Michael Dell, memo to staff, 25 April 2007

blocks.text: __He dropped the idea that made him famous once the numbers proved it had stopped working.__ In 2007, Dell went back into retail stores, which it had walked out of in 1994. By early 2008 it was in over 10,000 retail outlets. It moved away from building every PC to order, and looked to partners for more of its assembly. In India and other emerging markets, it opened plants of its own.

The human cost was real. Dell promised to cut 10 percent of its workforce, about 8,800 people. It closed its Austin desktop plant, with about 900 jobs lost. In January 2009, it moved European manufacturing to Poland, cutting 1,900 of 3,000 jobs in Limerick, Ireland, a country where it ranked itself the largest exporter. In October 2009 it said it would close its North Carolina plant, with 905 jobs lost.
The rise of Lenovo and the fall of the stock

It was not enough. Lenovo and HP kept taking PC share, and then the iPhone and iPad made people ask if anyone needed a PC at all. A court later summed up the three threats he saw on his return: cheap PC makers like Lenovo, smartphones and tablets, and cloud storage from companies like Amazon. His answer was the shopping spree you read about in the last chapter.

Wall Street did not buy it. Inside the company, a January 2011 analysis valued the shares at $22 to $27. On the market they sold for about $14. During the first half of 2012, they fell from about $18 to about $12, and that October they hit $9.66. Dell complained that the market just did not get it. __That gap, between what he thought his company was worth and what strangers would pay, would become the biggest opportunity of his life.__

blocks.text: The idea did not start with him. In ==June 2012==, Staley Cates of Southeastern Asset Management, Dell's biggest outside shareholder, asked Michael Dell if he would consider a management buyout. That is when a company's leader joins investors to buy all the shares and take it off the stock market. The next month he met Egon Durban of the buyout firm Silver Lake at a Fortune conference in Aspen. In August, the two talked again in Hawaii, where both had vacation homes.

He also went to his friend George Roberts of the buyout giant KKR, who said that if the numbers worked, KKR would want in. Then he did the part that protects a founder and everyone else: he called the board's lead independent director, Alex Mandl, and told him. He promised not to hire an adviser without first telling the board. The directors formed a special committee with full power over the process, and he left the room.
Tell the board first, before the bankers. Process matters when the lawyers come.

This was to be a leveraged buyout, which means buying a company mostly with borrowed money, and repaying it from the company's own cash. The bids came in on 23 October 2012, when the stock was $9.35. Silver Lake offered $11.22 to $12.16 a share, and KKR offered $12 to $13. Then the buyers started to run. KKR left on 3 December, saying it could not get its arms around the risks of the PC business. TPG looked and said no on 23 December.

Silver Lake raised its bid to $12.70, and the committee said no. It then held out for $13.75. Durban called Mandl and offered $13.25, and when Mandl refused, Durban threatened to walk away. Mandl told him to go ahead. __A good board works for the shareholders, not the founder, and sometimes its job is to tell him no.__

To break the deadlock, Michael Dell agreed to take less for his own shares than everyone else would get. That let Silver Lake reach ==$13.65== a share for the public, and the deal was signed on 5 February 2013. Microsoft came in with a $2 billion loan. It was a premium of 37 percent over the average price of the previous 90 days. Many shareholders still felt it was far too low.
